title: Is prompt engineering still relevant to vibe coding?
author: keixxxxxx
selftext:
Over the past year, I've started to feel that most of the conventional prompts commonly shared online have become largely unnecessary.

I'm talking about things like assigning the AI a specific role, adding elaborate instructions about how it should respond, or using various prompt templates to supposedly improve its output. I'm not referring to specifying the tech stack or technical requirements.

These prompts are still widely used, but personally, I've rarely found them to make any meaningful difference.

I also think instructions like "be objective" can be counterproductive. They often result in cherry-picked arguments or simply presenting two opposing extremes as equally valid. That's not objectivity.

What's your experience? Do you still find these kinds of prompts useful?

comments.author: do-sieg
comments.body:
It was a fad. True AI dev today is building an environment, skills, etc.
The models are good enough to understand your intent based on the context, and can fill up gaps in your instruction, guess what you really intended to say if you're vague, and can even ask to make sure.

replies.author: Visual_Internal_6312
replies.body: It depends. If you want to have more or less same behavior across harnesses and across different models, then it's still relevant. Also not all is coding, models are great at roleplay after all

comments.author: petateom
comments.body:
IMO for image/video generation is useful, but it's better to have a library of prompts.

For coding if you want to do properly you need to review and ask for a certain architecture.

comments.author: HeartlandDrifter
comments.body:
Prompt engineering is mostly just learning how to communicate more clearly with the model. But, with agents, most of this is done for you by the system prompt of the harness.

That said, "why did you delete that file!?" Because you told it the file was bad and to fix it. Deleting it was quicker than editing it. Problem solved.

Prompt engineering now looks more like setting conditions for tasks. "Here's your folder, don't go outside of it." "Edit line 17 from X to Y." "The webpage has a graphical bug in [specific spot] of the screen, that part needs to be fixed to be made uniform with the rest of it."

If you aren't being specific, then you are ignoring the oldest rule of prompt engineering: Don't give the model room to interpret, then complain about unexpected results.

replies.author: Visual_Internal_6312
replies.body: Context engineering is still alive and kicking although harnesses will do most of the heavy lifting.

comments.author: Beginning-Bet7824
comments.body:
I have been a gamedev for 7 years, working with early LLMs and diffusion models, and I have never used those "magic prompts".  
In the last month or so I finally gave up on the coding part entirely, letting AI just do its magic. But that doesn't mean that my coding experience is worthless.  
  
Often AI struggle to debug stuff, due to limitation in especially video, as screenshots may not be able to se flickering f.ex.   
  
Here my coding knowledge becomes valuable as I can guide the AI to explore possibilities that it wouldnt be able to identify directly itself. 

I think that exact wording and utter specific prompts has never been more than hype for non technical people that is tossed around the internet, as AI models work more in semantic that in token space, and only cares about the upper level meaning of the sentences.

That being said, "make me a game" and "Make be a game with xxx and yyy and zzz .... ect" would give you different results, but that has more to do with specifics than "engineered" phracing.

comments.author: Radiant_Mind33
comments.body:
Ya the models were always hard coded to behave a certain way no matter what you told them. 

Models used to mimic you very well but that was clearly unhealthy for a lot of people. I thought my mimic was badass, but I was clearly just drinking some kind of kool aid too.

comments.author: azzaisme
comments.body: They built the prompt engineering into the model

comments.author: BlobbyMcBlobber
comments.body:
No. Prompt engineering died a long time ago.

Context engineering is also on its way out. The models are just really good at using tools and finding the information they need. It still helps that you know something about context engineering, but it's less of a big deal.

None of these things earned their "engineering" tag in my opinion.

comments.author: Only-Cheetah-9579
comments.body: it was never really a thing, nobody did it correctly and nowadays just talking to your AI as a manager is enough
